When investors discuss the major artificial intelligence (AI) hyperscalers, Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) sometimes falls to the wayside. However, its Copilot AI platform is rapidly growing and might be its secret weapon in the AI arms race. Copilot is becoming a widely used AI application in the business world, mainly due to its ability to keep companies' internal, proprietary data private. This is becoming an issue for some places, and with Copilot maintaining data security, it's an easy one for IT departments to recommend.
But is it enough to make Microsoft a buy? Let's take a look.

Microsoft is benefiting from the AI arms race in three ways
Microsoft has three different ways it can benefit from the AI arms race.
The first, as discussed above, is its Copilot platform. A free version of Copilot is available with all plans, but integrations with some of Microsoft's other apps are a paid add-on. During Microsoft's latest quarter, Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats. That's not an insignificant revenue contributor, and it shows that it's growing in popularity.

How Much Revenue Visibility Does Microsoft’s Backlog Really Provide?
Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) ended fiscal 2026 with $678 billion of commercial remaining performance obligations. That total offers substantial visibility, but its investment value depends on when revenue arrives, which customers account for it and what Microsoft must spend to serve them. Treating the whole amount as near-term sales would overstate the protection it provides.
At the September 30 market-data snapshot, Microsoft's market capitalization was about $3.86 trillion, around 29 times trailing earnings on an equity basis and roughly 57 times trailing free cash flow. Such a valuation makes the quality and timing of future contracted business more relevant than the size of the headline alone.
How much cash does contracted growth leave after the infrastructure bill? Our Microsoft-versus-Amazon analysis compares the conversion of cloud investment into profit. OpenAI's role adds another question: our examination of the missing profit figure behind Microsoft's large OpenAI revenue stream shows why revenue visibility and shareholder returns need separate tests.
How Much Revenue Visibility Does Microsoft's Backlog Really Provide?
On the July 29 earnings call, management said the weighted average duration of remaining obligations was 2.3 years, with approximately 30% expected to be recognized in the following 12 months. Thirty percent of $678 billion is about $203.4 billion. That is expected recognition from the existing backlog, not an extra $203.4 billion layered on top of the company's normal revenue forecast.
The distinction matters because future revenue also comes from renewals, new contracts and usage that is not captured in the same snapshot. Microsoft's fiscal 2026 revenue was $331.8 billion, spanning businesses beyond this commercial measure. Dividing scheduled backlog recognition by consolidated revenue can give scale, but cannot produce a precise coverage ratio for all future sales.
The backlog grew 84%, while growth excluding OpenAI was 25%. That contrast identifies a source of concentration rather than disproving demand elsewhere. Management said sequential backlog growth came entirely from customers outside frontier labs and that nearly 90% of full-year fiscal 2026 Microsoft Cloud revenue was outside that group. Existing revenue breadth and future contractual concentration can therefore tell different stories.
Contracted revenue still needs profitable capacity
September 15 short interest was 67,346,414 shares, about 0.91% of float, with 3.7 days to cover. The small float percentage makes it weak evidence for a crowded directional trade.
Insider Monkey's hedge fund database recorded 273 Microsoft holders in Q2 2026, down from 282 in Q1. Arrowstreet increased its common-share position 14% to 27,659,541 shares. The divergence between broader participation and one manager's position is historical; it cannot be read as a response to the July 29 backlog disclosure.
Microsoft generated $182.94 billion of operating cash flow in fiscal 2026 and paid $115.95 billion for property and equipment. Simple free cash flow was about $66.99 billion. The approximately $3.81 trillion equity valuation equaled about 57 times that amount, a cash yield near 1.8%.
Backlog can help justify building capacity because it reduces uncertainty about customer demand. It does not remove the equipment cost, energy expense, depreciation or customer-credit exposure. A long contract is more valuable when the associated assets earn good returns throughout its term.
As an illustrative sensitivity, $100 billion of sustainable annual free cash flow would put the current equity value at about 38 times cash flow. At $125 billion, the multiple would be roughly 30.5. Reaching either level requires operating cash growth to exceed the ongoing cash needed for infrastructure, or investment intensity to decline as capacity fills. Neither follows automatically from an 84% increase in obligations.
The strongest bullish case is that Microsoft's broad customer base, contracted demand and expanding cloud platform create both growth and high utilization of new infrastructure. The bearish case is that a larger share of backlog involves expensive, concentrated workloads whose cash returns arrive slowly. If those customers change their deployment plans, long duration may become a risk exposure as well as a source of visibility.
Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) has considerable contracted demand, with recognition timing and customer breadth shaping its value. The backlog becomes more persuasive when deployed capacity converts it into growing cash after investment. Contract growth that consistently outruns cash returns would leave the price dependent on a longer and less certain payoff.

OpenAI’s Future IPO Keeps Me Buying Microsoft
Microsoft holds a stake in OpenAI that no public market has ever priced, and one investor argues that gap between the stock and the business is exactly where the opportunity lives.

I keep buying Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction), and every quarter gives me another reason to add more. The reason I bring up most at dinner is OpenAI. Microsoft owns roughly 27% of the company behind ChatGPT. That stake was valued at approximately $135 billion when the partnership was restructured. One day the stake will get a public price, and I want my shares in place before then.
Paper Value Wall Street Still Can’t Price
OpenAI is reportedly aiming a valuation of about $1.2 trillion, and its listing now points toward 2027. If OpenAI lists near that figure, a 27% stake would be worth about $324 billion on paper before dilution. That equals roughly 8.5% of Microsoft’s $3.81 trillion market cap. Right now that value shows up mostly as an accounting line. A public market would price it every trading day.
I could wait and buy OpenAI directly at its IPO. I’d rather own it through Microsoft. Microsoft keeps IP rights to OpenAI models through 2032, including post-AGI models. OpenAI also signed to buy an additional $250 billion of Azure services. An OpenAI shareholder owns one model company. I own the stake, the cloud signed, and a platform that gets paid no matter which model wins. Polymarket traders give Microsoft a 0.56 probability of ending the year with a higher valuation than Anthropic and OpenAI combined.
First, Microsoft keeps growing at huge scale. Fiscal 2026 revenue reached $331.84 billion, up 17.8%, and Azure passed $100 billion for the first time. For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, management guided Azure growth to approximately 45% in constant currency.
Second, the backlog. Commercial remaining performance obligations, meaning signed revenue not yet recognized, reached $678 billion, up 84%. Without OpenAI, that backlog still grew 25%. Nearly 90% of full-year Microsoft Cloud revenue came from customers outside frontier model companies. The core business stands on its own, and OpenAI adds upside.
Third, the quality of the business. Operating margin is 46.78%, return on equity is 34.04%, debt-to-equity is 0.29, with interest coverage at 50.88x. Microsoft returned over $43 billion to shareholders in fiscal 2026. The 0.69% dividend yield is small, so I own this stock for the compounding behind the payout. At 28x earnings, I think the price for that profile is fair.
The spending concerns me most. Capital expenditures for fiscal 2026 reached $115.95 billion, up 79.6%, and free cash flow fell 6.5%. Management expects fiscal 2027 capex of about $175 billion. OpenAI losses also hit GAAP earnings: $3.1 billion in the first quarter of fiscal 2026, compared with $523 million a year earlier. And the IPO date keeps slipping.
My case still holds because demand keeps exceeding supply. On the July 29 call, CFO Amy Hood said “Demand continues to exceed available supply”. She called the data center investment “quite flexible”. Microsoft also expects to stay free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027.
Over the past year the stock moved -0.51%. Over the same period, revenue rose, the backlog grew, and Copilot passed 30 million paid seats. That gap between the stock and the business is my window. When OpenAI finally prices, I want my Microsoft shares already sitting in my account, compounding while everyone else waits for the IPO.

Microsoft Corporation stock (ISIN US5949181045) is trading near its recent highs after the software giant reported a strong fiscal fourth quarter in late July, posting revenue of USD 90.01 billion and earnings per share of USD 4.74 that topped Wall Street expectations according to MarketBeat on July 29, 2026. As of the last completed trading day before the Labor Day holiday on September 4, 2026, market data indicate that Microsoft’s share price on Nasdaq was close to its 52-week high, reflecting investor confidence in the company’s AI-driven growth.
In its fiscal fourth quarter ended in late July 2026, Microsoft generated revenue of USD 90.01 billion, exceeding consensus estimates of around USD 87.62 billion reported by MarketBeat. That represents approximately 17.7 percent year-over-year growth for the quarter, highlighting how demand across cloud and productivity products continues to expand. Earnings per share reached USD 4.74 versus a consensus of USD 4.24, meaning Microsoft delivered USD 0.50 EPS above expectations in the quarter, a gap that underscores ongoing operating leverage in its software and cloud businesses.
According to a recent analysis on Yahoo Finance dated September 7, 2026, the July results marked a record fiscal fourth quarter for Microsoft, with Azure revenue surpassing USD 100 billion annually after growing 43 percent during the quarter. That annualized Azure revenue figure, combined with double-digit overall growth, shows how AI workloads are translating into concrete cloud spending and positions Microsoft as a key beneficiary of the latest generative AI cycle. For investors, the notable point is that the company is turning heavy AI infrastructure investments into higher revenue rather than margin pressure, at least in the near term.
The July earnings report triggered a clear reaction in Microsoft stock, with the share price jumping roughly 17 percent in the period following the results as investors rewarded the company’s AI execution, according to Yahoo Finance on September 7, 2026. That move pushed the stock toward the upper end of its recent trading range and close to its 52-week high, signaling that the market now prices in stronger cloud growth and a premium for Microsoft’s strategic positioning in AI. While exact valuation multiples depend on the latest intraday data, this post-earnings rally illustrates how quickly sentiment can shift when a large-cap technology name demonstrates above-consensus growth and clear traction in a key theme such as AI.
At the same time, the broader US equity market has seen periods of volatility around interest rate expectations and inflation data, and Microsoft’s share performance is partly framed by those macro factors. With Azure growth accelerating and the company forecasting substantial capital expenditures for fiscal 2027 in support of AI infrastructure, the stock embodies both opportunity and risk: high growth potential but also sensitivity to any slowdown in enterprise spending or changes in the cost of capital. For long-term shareholders, the balance between sustained double-digit revenue growth and disciplined cost management remains central to the investment case.
Guidance, capex and the next earnings date
Ahead of its next quarterly report, market commentary compiled by TradingKey on September 6, 2026 highlights consensus expectations for Microsoft’s upcoming fiscal quarter: around USD 87.67 billion in revenue and USD 4.24 in EPS for Q4 of fiscal 2026. While those figures are estimates rather than final reported results, they provide a benchmark that investors will use to evaluate whether Microsoft can maintain the strong trajectory seen in the July quarter. In addition, guidance discussed in recent coverage points to fiscal 2027 capital expenditures in the range of USD 255 billion to USD 260 billion, which would represent roughly a 35 percent increase from about USD 190 billion spent in calendar 2026. This step-up in investment underscores how aggressively Microsoft is building out its AI and cloud infrastructure to meet expected demand.
Looking ahead, the next major catalyst for Microsoft stock is its forthcoming earnings release, which market calendars and previews indicate is scheduled for late October 2026, after the close of US trading. The accompanying conference call is expected to start around 5:30 PM Eastern Time on the reporting day, giving investors and analysts the opportunity to assess updated guidance, Azure growth trends and any changes to the company’s capex plans. With the July quarter having delivered both a top-line beat and EPS outperformance, the bar for the next print is higher, and any deviation from the current consensus on growth or margins could quickly impact the share price.
Risks around AI spending and macro conditions
Despite the current strength, several risk factors accompany the bullish narrative around Microsoft stock. One key risk is the sheer scale of planned AI-related capital expenditure: an increase of roughly one-third from calendar 2026 levels implies a heavy upfront investment that must be matched by sustained demand and pricing power in Azure and related services. If enterprise AI adoption were to slow or shift toward lower-margin offerings, the returns on this capex could come under scrutiny, which in turn might weigh on the stock. In addition, intense competition from other hyperscale cloud providers and AI platform companies means Microsoft must continuously innovate to defend its share of high-value workloads.
Macro conditions provide another layer of uncertainty. Analysts and market observers note that upcoming US inflation data and Federal Reserve decisions on interest rates will influence overall risk appetite, including for large-cap technology stocks such as Microsoft. A higher-for-longer interest rate environment tends to pressure valuation multiples for growth stocks, and any surprise in inflation figures could lead to short-term volatility in the share price even if company-specific fundamentals remain strong. For investors, monitoring both Microsoft’s execution on AI and the broader rate backdrop is essential when interpreting the stock’s moves around upcoming earnings dates.
Azure and Microsoft 365 as core products
Within Microsoft’s portfolio, the Azure cloud platform and Microsoft 365 productivity suite stand out as the main drivers of the recent earnings beat. Azure’s reported 43 percent quarterly growth in the latest fiscal quarter and more than USD 100 billion in annualized revenue underscore its central role in the company’s strategy to capture AI-related demand, according to Yahoo Finance. Many new generative AI services, including integrations with OpenAI’s ChatGPT-based models, run on Azure infrastructure, which supports high-margin consumption of compute and storage. The continued expansion of these services is a key reason why investors have rewarded Microsoft stock in the wake of the July earnings.
Microsoft 365, which bundles Office applications with collaboration tools like Teams and security features, contributes recurring subscription revenue that stabilizes the company’s overall earnings profile. As enterprises adopt AI capabilities within productivity software, such as AI copilots embedded in Office applications, these products increasingly link day-to-day usage to Microsoft’s broader AI platform. For shareholders, this combination of fast-growing Azure revenue and steady Microsoft 365 subscription income provides a diversified earnings base supporting the high level of investment in AI infrastructure.

Daily trading volume in Microsoft shares typically reaches tens of millions of shares on Nasdaq, and the last completed trading day before the holiday period was no exception, with robust liquidity enabling institutional investors to adjust positions in response to the July earnings beat and evolving AI expectations. For retail investors, this deep liquidity and tight bid-ask spreads help reduce transaction costs when entering or exiting positions around key events such as earnings releases and macro data prints. The combination of high liquidity, strong fundamental growth, and a clearly defined AI narrative is a major reason why Microsoft stock continues to occupy a central role in many diversified equity portfolios.

Microsoft won’t admit its New Outlook is terrible, but it knows plenty of users still prefer Outlook Classic. And to address this, Microsoft has just cloned Outlook Classic’s look and turned it into a theme for New Outlook, in the hope that holdouts will finally switch. Yes, you can now make New Outlook look like the classic one, although it’s still a web app.
There’s a new optional setting in New Outlook for Windows 11 and Windows 10 that allows you to use this classic design as a “theme.” Microsoft began rolling it out in August 2026, and it finally showed up on my PC.
I went to New Outlook’s Settings > General > Appearance and turned on “Enable classic Outlook style.” Once enabled, New Outlook looked a lot closer to Outlook Classic.
As soon as you tick the box, New Outlook tells you that “some settings aren’t available in classic Outlook style,” and the entire Themes section, including Copilot themes, image backgrounds, and accent colors, gets greyed out. So you can either have the classic look or your custom theme, not both.
That doesn’t change the fact that New Outlook is still a web app running in an Edge-powered container, but it’s also why these themes are so well cooked.
Microsoft can easily customize how New Outlook looks because it’s a website at the end of the day, so a bit of CSS and JavaScript can take you from the new design to the one you loved all these years.
In our tests, Windows Latest observed changes across New Outlook’s interface to make it resemble Outlook Classic. For example, I noticed that the title bar, icons, folder list, and ribbon all changed to look more like the classic version. This is the New Outlook running Outlook Classic, and you’d be surprised how identical it looks:
Even the blue patterned title bar, which is one of the flagship design aspects of New Outlook, is gone. In light mode, it’s replaced with a plain background, again matching the classic version.
Microsoft has also added two small buttons to the top-left corner of the title bar, Send/Receive (sync) and Undo, which mimic Outlook Classic’s Quick Access Toolbar. Even the Outlook logo switches to the older multicolor icon.
You’ve also got an updated navigation bar, but there are not a lot of changes here. Microsoft has made the background darker in dark mode, and you’ve got monochrome outlines for the Mail, Calendar, People, and other app icons. We’re getting a new Calendar view as well, with a classic theme:
Right now, New Outlook has colorful icons, so by just changing the icons and making the background darker, Outlook Classic is being recreated.
The Calendar ribbon also borrows from Outlook Classic. You get “Today” and “Next 7 Days” buttons under a new “Go to” group, and an “Add” button under “Manage Calendars,” instead of New Outlook’s Filter, Split view, and Print buttons. There’s a Folder tab in Calendar too.
In a support document seen by Windows Latest, Microsoft confirmed it’s paying attention to iconography and typography to bridge the gap between the two apps.
“When enabled, the setting applies coordinated changes across the Outlook experience, including visual styling, layout, typography, icons, and selected interactions,” Microsoft explained. “This update is designed to help users who are transitioning from classic Outlook by providing a more familiar experience while maintaining the capabilities of the new Outlook.”
Microsoft has also redesigned the mail folder list, so it looks more compact, like the Outlook Classic version. You’ll no longer see icons beside individual folders such as Inbox, Drafts, and Sent Items.
The text is smaller, and the Favorites section now shows the full account name next to each Inbox instead of cutting it off. I also spotted a new “Shared with me” section under my work account, which lists the shared mailboxes I have access to, just like Outlook Classic.
The email list has also picked up one of my favorite Outlook Classic habits. Instead of grouping emails by month, New Outlook now groups them into “Yesterday,” “Wednesday,” “Sunday,” “Last Week,” “Two Weeks Ago,” and “Last Month,” and every email shows the day next to the date, like “Wed 9/30/2026.”
And the most noticeable part, the ribbon, has some familiar design changes, too. For example, if you’re in the mail view, you can see Send / Receive and Folder tabs alongside File, Home, View, and Help. The blue “New mail” button also becomes a neutral “New Email” button with a separate “New Items” dropdown, and copies Outlook Classic’s iconography.
The Send / Receive tab is pretty barebones right now. It only has two buttons, “Send/Receive All Folders” and “Work offline.” The Folder tab has New Folder, New Search Folder, Add to Favorites, and Folder pane options.
On the Home tab, you’ll also find a “Groups” section with New Group and Browse Groups, and a “Send to OneNote” button, both of which were part of Outlook Classic’s ribbon.
The View tab is different, too. It now has “Use Tighter Spacing,” “Conversation Settings,” and a “To-Do Bar” option, which is another throwback to Outlook Classic.
Last but not least, if you open the compose window, you’ll notice the same Outlook Classic-like design treatment. For example, you’ll see Message, Insert, Format Text, Draw, and Options tabs across the top, with formatting controls in the ribbon below.
I could continue listing everything I spotted, but it’s quite obvious Microsoft has done a pretty good job of bringing Outlook Classic’s look to New Outlook. Now, it just needs one thing: bring back the native Outlook app because whatever we have right now is still a RAM-hogging Edge instance!

Microsoft (MSFT) Stock Rises as Oppenheimer Raises Price Target on Copilot Overhaul
Microsoft (MSFT) stock rose 4% after Oppenheimer raised its price target to $570 following a major Copilot enterprise overhaul.
By Trader EdgeSeptember 26, 20264 Mins Read
Microsoft stock rose as much as 4% on Friday, hitting $516.39 in afternoon trading.
Oppenheimer analyst Brian Schwartz raised his MSFT price target to $570 from $515, keeping an Outperform rating.
Microsoft merged its consumer and workplace Copilot assistants into one enterprise-focused app.
The new app is built around three tools: a home chat hub, a coding tool, and an agent called Autopilot.
Microsoft stock is up 7% year to date, well behind the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund’s 37% gain.
Microsoft stock climbed on Friday, rising as much as 4% to reach $516.39 in afternoon trading. The move came after Oppenheimer raised its price target on the tech giant and Microsoft rolled out a major overhaul of its Copilot app.
Oppenheimer analyst Brian Schwartz lifted his price target on Microsoft to $570 from $515. He kept his Outperform rating in place. Schwartz pointed to customers increasingly standardizing on Microsoft as their main enterprise AI platform.
Stifel analyst Brad Reback also raised his outlook. He upgraded Microsoft from hold to buy and pushed his price target up to $575 from $530. That target points to roughly 11% upside from Friday’s closing price.
Technology stocks broadly helped lift the market on Friday. The Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund, which holds Microsoft as one of its largest positions, rose 0.8%. The S&P 500 was up a smaller 0.2%.
Microsoft merged its consumer and workplace Copilot assistants into a single app built for businesses. That move ends the company’s push to build a personal AI companion for everyday users.
Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna explained the thinking at a preview event. He said the company isn’t trying to build a personal companion app, and instead wants to help people get work done.
The redesigned app centers on three tools. A home hub combines chat with task delegation, letting users edit Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files directly inside the app.
A second tool, built on GitHub Copilot technology, lets non-technical staff build apps and workflows using plain language. It runs inside a sandbox that a company’s IT team controls.
The third tool, called Autopilot, acts as a persistent agent living inside a company’s own cloud setup. It can handle multi-step background tasks without constant human input.
Microsoft’s pricing now follows a split model. Everyday chat use comes with a fixed subscription fee, while longer agentic tasks get billed on a pay-as-you-go basis.
This shift changes how predictable Microsoft’s AI revenue will be. The company has more than 30 million paid Copilot enterprise subscriptions, which gave it a steady, seat-based revenue base.
Usage-based billing ties part of that revenue to how often customers actually run the agent tools. That’s a different setup than counting fixed seats each month.
Not everyone gets Microsoft’s full attention here. Alphabet continues targeting consumer AI users through Gemini, and OpenAI does the same with ChatGPT. Alphabet stock was up 0.68% to $344.70 on Friday.
Microsoft stock has lagged its own sector for most of 2026. Shares are up 7% year to date, compared to a 37% gain for the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund over the same stretch.
Schwartz flagged some risks alongside his price target increase. He pointed to AI disruption and the possibility that companies pull forward their enterprise tech spending, both of which could weigh on Microsoft’s growth path.
Microsoft’s stock carries a Buy consensus among 55 analysts covering the company, with 14 rating it Strong Buy and 38 rating it Buy. Three analysts rate it Hold.
Microsoft closed Thursday at $497.93 before Friday’s rally. The stock’s 52-week range spans from $348.54 to $549.20.

On Wednesday morning, in a Manhattan press room containing about 50 reporters and union members, one of the largest teachers’ unions in the US announced an agreement with Microsoft that, among other things, prohibits the tech company from tracking student use of its AI tools and applying student and teacher data to train AI models.
The guidelines listed in the American Federation of Teachers’ deal with Microsoft apply to any school district “that desires the same principles” when forming their own customer agreements with the company and purchasing its AI products.
The union also gives Microsoft—and any other tech company that signs on (AFT President Randi Weingarten mentioned ongoing conversations with OpenAI and Anthropic during Wednesday’s announcement)—a 180-day deadline to delete records of AI data use from students and school districts on its active systems following a request.
Microsoft agreed not to use student and teacher data to train its AI — but there are exceptions. The guidelines point out “narrow safety and security” situations, including letting the company use “the minimum amount” of school user data to detect, prevent, investigate, or remediate harm to users or security threats to its AI products and retain it “for as long as reasonably necessary.”
The contract also lists “contractual remedies” for school districts that sign on, such as the ability to pause or discontinue Microsoft’s deployment of its AI systems if the company commits any material breaches of its agreement obligations.
The current guidelines do not present explicit, quantifiable rules for what is considered remediation by a “reasonable” time—it’s something that both Microsoft and the customer will “engage in good faith” to come up with.
When I asked Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith about specific guidelines on how an accountability process will work if Microsoft fails to comply with remediation on Wednesday, he largely dodged the question, saying that Microsoft has to publish reports that provide transparency to the AFT and school districts and have tight deadlines for fixes.
“Obviously, this [remediation process] becomes part of our broader contract with each school district, and all of those [existing] contracts already have built-in remedies,” Smith told Mother Jones. “I think that there’s just an unprecedented amount of transparency associated with the commitments that are in this agreement.”
When I asked again about specific steps that will be taken if Microsoft fails to comply, Smith said they are “connected back into the provisions that we have in our contract with each school district. Those can vary.”
“Mostly, what I find is that what people want when something goes wrong is just to go fix it. People don’t want to end up with more time with lawyers,” he continued. “That’s always an option if somebody wants to take action, but let’s just fix problems when they arise.”
While accountability applies to how each school district will work with Microsoft in the near future, the company seemingly not holding discussions now raises questions about the feasibility of contract enforceability.
Microsoft, and other companies like Google, have a history of promoting their AI products to schools and educators, and a healthy skepticism is needed when relying in part on tech companies to police AI and previous failures of implementing educational technology.
Weingarten and Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers representing New York City public school educators and others, who were also taking questions immediately following the announcement, did not respond to the question.
The contract comes a week after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a one-year moratorium on AI use for elementary and middle school students in the city’s public schools, and the Los Angeles Unified School District announced restrictions to generative AI platforms for all students for the 2026-27 school year.
The AFT’s contract with Microsoft contains the sentence “When in doubt, protect the student.” on the bottom of each of the 31 pages. But exactly how any of these policies around AI use in schools will actually work remains unclear.

Deciding between Accenture (ACN -6.31%) and Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) requires choosing between a dominant professional services provider and a global leader in software platforms as both companies race toward an AI-driven future.
Accenture thrives as the primary partner for digital transformation projects, while Microsoft provides the underlying cloud infrastructure and productivity tools that businesses use daily. Though they operate in different niches, both are considered foundational investments for those looking to capitalize on the ongoing expansion of the enterprise technology landscape.
As a prominent name among tech stocks, Accenture provides essential professional services, helping enterprises and governments navigate complex shifts in technology and strategy. With approximately 814,000 employees globally, it serves roughly 9,000 clients, including a vast majority of the Fortune Global 500. The firm leverages deep ecosystem partnerships with the largest cloud providers to integrate specialized solutions for its five major industry groups, which include financial services and health and public service.
In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2026, revenue reached nearly $74.2 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 6.5% compared to the prior year. This steady expansion supported a net income of roughly $8.5 billion for the period. The net margin of close to 11.5% reflects a slight improvement over the previous fiscal years, indicating a consistent ability to generate profit from its global consulting and outsourcing operations.
As of its August 2026 balance sheet, the company reported a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.3x. This metric, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, suggests a conservative approach to borrowing. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations, was nearly 1.4x, while free cash flow, calculated as cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures, reached roughly $11.6 billion for the year.
Microsoft focuses on providing the infrastructure for the modern digital economy through cloud services, AI-powered productivity tools, and personal computing hardware. The business relies heavily on Azure and Microsoft 365, which serve a massive spectrum of users from individual consumers to multinational corporations. High-profile investments in AI, particularly via its Copilot offerings, remain central to its efforts to drive growth across all business segments.
In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2026, the company generated revenue of nearly $331.8 billion, a robust 17.8% increase over its FY 2025 results. This performance led to net income of approximately $133.7 billion for the fiscal year. The net margin reached close to 40.3%, highlighting the significant profitability of its software-centric model when compared to more labor-intensive services businesses.
As of its June 2026 balance sheet, the company maintained a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 0.3x. This metric compares total debt against shareholder equity, and a lower value typically indicates less financial risk. Its current ratio was approximately 1.2x, while free cash flow for the year, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was exceptionally strong at nearly $67.0 billion.
Accenture faces significant competition in the global services market, where rapid technological shifts in AI could disrupt traditional pricing models. Geopolitical risks are also present due to the company reliance on global delivery centers in regions like India and the Philippines. Additionally, it recently addressed a $25 million settlement with the Department of Justice regarding federal contracting practices.
Microsoft is currently navigating several legal challenges, including securities fraud class action lawsuits involving its AI and Copilot claims. The company faces intense competition from other cloud hyperscalers like Amazon or Alphabet. Furthermore, it is under scrutiny from global regulators regarding antitrust concerns and is managing a large-scale tax audit with the IRS.
Accenture offers a much lower valuation on both an earnings and sales basis, while Microsoft commands a significant premium for its faster growth.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
I'd go with Microsoft, and it's not a close call. After its most recent results, the case for it has rarely looked stronger. Azure growth accelerated for the fifth consecutive quarter, Copilot paid seats more than doubled, and the company raised its full-year outlook with confidence that its AI strategy is working at scale. The AI build-out is now running partly on Microsoft's infrastructure, partly on its software, and increasingly on its Copilot tools.
To its credit, Accenture is building a credible AI consulting business that enterprises are paying for. Revenue grew at a healthy pace, earnings beat estimates, and the AI consulting opportunity keeps expanding as enterprises need help deploying the tools Microsoft and others are building. For investors who want steady, professional services exposure to the AI transformation, it has its appeal.
But Accenture's stock sold off after its most recent earnings despite a decent quarter, weighed down by weaker bookings and a cautious near-term tone. When a stock drops on good news, it usually means the market expects the bar to keep moving higher. Microsoft is setting the bar. Accenture is helping enterprises clear it. For a long-term investor, owning the platform is the stronger starting point.

Why Microsoft (MSFT) Stock Is Getting Fresh Price Target Upgrades This Week
Microsoft (MSFT) stock rises after Oppenheimer lifts its price target to $570 and Cantor Fitzgerald raises to $608, citing Azure and Copilot growth.

Oppenheimer raised its Microsoft price target from $515 to $570, maintaining an Outperform rating

Microsoft (MSFT) stock climbed in Tuesday’s pre-market trading after Oppenheimer raised its price target to $570 from $515. The stock was trading at $501.61, up 4% year-to-date. The new target implies roughly 14% upside from that level.
Oppenheimer analyst Brian Schwartz maintained an Outperform rating on the stock. The upgrade came after a recent visit to Microsoft’s headquarters.
Schwartz said his “acceleration with capital discipline” thesis for Microsoft remains intact. He sees the company growing without letting spending spiral out of control.
He expects Azure and Microsoft 365 Commercial to keep their growth momentum going into fiscal year 2027. He pointed to stronger Copilot monetization as a key part of that story, along with more compute capacity coming online.

Cantor Fitzgerald Adds to the Bullish Case

Schwartz did not ignore the downside. He warned that some enterprise IT spending may have been pulled forward into the second half of 2026, which could soften Azure and M365 growth heading into 2027.

pages.title: Microsoft using wetlands and native gardens to 'camouflage' 20-plus data center sites by blending them into nature
pages.text:
Top Stories:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.
Microsoft's "biomimicry" program is reshaping the land around its data centers with restored wetlands and native gardens to help the buildings blend into local ecosystems at 20-plus sites, reports The Verge. Critics question the company's motives after recent energy deals, such as a 20-year deal inked in June to buy power from a planned Chevron gas plant in West Texas. Public Citizen's Texas director, Adrian Shelley, called the plan "basically lipstick on a pig."
Microsoft says the approach is now part of all new projects in the U.S. The goal is to blend "data centers into the natural landscape" at sites across the United States and Germany, gauging community input and using ecological research to map the local environment. Microsoft's team uses a tool called Ecosystem Intelligence, which runs on Azure and scores various features of the site, including water quality, biodiversity, and noise abatement.
Solutions, according to Microsoft's director of global land strategy, Kaitlin Chuzi, are customized to the local habitat and should restore what was lost, while plant buffers quiet data center humming and help "minimize the visual impact on communities near our data centers." Named sites include Mecklenburg County, Virginia; Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin; East Point, Georgia; Bedburg, Germany; and other projects in Ohio, North Carolina, and Wyoming.
The Mount Pleasant site, home to Fairwater, which Microsoft calls the "world's most powerful AI data center," has 100 acres of prairie and forest in a Lamparek Creek restoration with the Root-Pike Watershed Initiative Network. Its executive director, Dave Giordano, told the outlet that Microsoft developed its stormwater ponds with forebays to retain sediment, one of a number of accommodations for the environment. "Not all data center companies are the same," he said. It is a living example of the company's answer to AI data center backlash.
San Antonio District 6 Councilmember Ric Galvan told the outlet that there are more than a dozen data centers in his district, with more proposed. He cited concerns about the impact on traffic and the environment, including tree removal, following a 2022 approval of a Microsoft plan to remove 2,642 trees from a 33-acre tract for a data center.
Microsoft spokesperson Jennifer Lyons, however, said in an email to the outlet that the company is investing in more than 400 acres of woodland and pollinator prairie restoration in San Antonio and intends to leave the "land more productive than we received it." Galvan said Microsoft may be "covering their bases," which he said is fine if residents' concerns are addressed. He proposed a moratorium on new data centers in August, backed by Public Citizen, but the council opted against a blanket pause and is weighing zoning rules instead, with a vote scheduled for Oct. 15.
Shelley also pointed to adjacent effects, specifically pollution from new gas plants built to supply energy for data centers. "I cannot really see any level of biomimicry investment that makes a gas plant a desirable neighbor," he told the outlet. Chevron says its plant would provide "approximately 2.67 gigawatts" of power if the plan goes through, with first power anticipated in 2028.
Meanwhile, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has paused approvals for data centers seeking to connect to the state's main power grid until regulators audit them. In September, he barred the state's environmental agency from issuing new data center permits until the audit is done. Water use, a common criticism, was only about 0.4% of the state's total from data centers in 2025, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). It projects water usage of 0.5% to 2.7% by 2030.
Emissions have risen by Microsoft's own accounting, too. Its 2026 Environmental Sustainability Report, released in July, puts the total up 25% in fiscal 2025, "driven primarily by the expansion of our datacenter infrastructure" and by Microsoft pausing its use of unbundled renewable energy certificates, a type of accounting credit. Microsoft has 2030 goals of becoming carbon negative and water positive, meeting the latter in fiscal 2025 by its own measure.
Holly Alpine, who led ecosystem restoration and climate resilience work near Microsoft's data centers until leaving in 2024, still sees a gap between data center buildouts and sustainability goals. Microsoft said in an email to the outlet that AI at a global scale must have "a range of energy solutions in the near term."
Microsoft had no clear answer when questioned if it would ever change its mind on a site. Chuzi called it "an ongoing learning process to understand what that means to be a good neighbor." HARC's Erin Kinney told the outlet the real test is how Microsoft calculates, tracks, and shares the benefits with communities. Accurate measurement would make it easier to have genuine cooperation moving forward so that both data center companies and local communities can come together to mitigate environmental impacts.

Microsoft vs. Johnson & Johnson: Which Dividend Will Pay You More in 10 Years?
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 8:30 AM PDT 5 min read
Microsoft vs. Johnson & Johnson: Which Dividend Will Pay You More in 10 Years? ©SteveLuker from Getty Images and Mungkhoodstudio via Canva
Microsoft just raised its quarterly dividend 8% to $0.98, and Johnson & Johnson raised its payout for the 64th straight year in April.
Johnson & Johnson yields about 2%, more than double Microsoft's 0.8%, but Microsoft has grown its dividend about twice as fast over the last five years.
Microsoft's cash dividend payout ratio is a well-covered 40% TTM but spikes to a risky 89% going forward as capital spending eats into free cash flow, against a steady 57% and 53% for Johnson & Johnson.
Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) just gave its shareholders a raise. On Sept. 15, its board raised the quarterly dividend 7 cents, or 8%, to $0.98 a share.
Whereas back in April, Johnson & Johnson (JNJ:NYSE) put out the kind of headline most companies can only dream of: "Johnson & Johnson Announces 64th Consecutive Year of Dividend Increase."
Both are dividend growers, with very different starting points. Microsoft grows fast from a small yield, and J&J grows slowly from a much bigger one. So if you're buying for income, which one will actually pay you more in 10 years?
Source: TIKR and company filings, prices at the Sept. 28, 2026 close; forward is consensus for each company's next fiscal year.
Microsoft's business is humming. Revenue rose 18% to $90.0 billion in its latest quarter, and CEO Satya Nadella pointed out that "Azure revenue surpassed $100 billion for the first time" this fiscal year.
The dividend has grown about 10% a year over the last five years, and free cash flow has covered it easily…
Microsoft (MSFT): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2026 (years to June) (TIKR)
And even after two straight years of falling free cash flow, $67 billion covers $26.5 billion of dividends with plenty to spare.
The catch is AI spending. Capital spending jumped about 80% to $116 billion in fiscal 2026, and analysts expect free cash flow to roughly halve next fiscal year, to $32.34 billion. That takes Microsoft's cash dividend payout ratio from 39.5% TTM to 89.2% forward. (Consensus does see free cash flow recovering to $45.81 billion the year after.)
For income, $10,000 in Microsoft today pays about $77 a year. If the dividend keeps growing at its 10-year pace of 9.7%, that's about $195 in year 10. So, call it a 2% yield on your cash today. Not amazing on its own, but of course you want to consider capital appreciation as well.
Johnson & Johnson: Big check, steady raises
J&J is growing too. Second-quarter sales rose 6.6% to $25.3 billion, and management raised its 2026 sales guidance to $101.1 billion at the midpoint. As CEO Joaquin Duato put it, J&J is "on track to meet our 2026 target of more than $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time in our Company's 140-year history."
The dividend grows more slowly: about 5% a year over the last five years, and this April's raise was 3.1%. But the starting check is much bigger. $10,000 in J&J today pays about $197 a year. At its 10-year growth rate of 5.7%, that's about $343 in year 10.
Johnson & Johnson (JNJ): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2015–2025 (TIKR)
Dividends paid rose about 52% over that stretch while free cash flow rose about 22%, a gap I'd keep an eye on.
Still, J&J's cash dividend payout ratio is 56.7% TTM and 53.0% forward, and net debt is just 0.81x EBITDA. The main risk is that dividend growth keeps slowing. Even at 3.1% a year, though, that $10,000 would pay about $267 in year 10.
So which dividend wins?
Ultimately, I have to go with Johnson & Johnson on this one. It pays more than 2.5 times as much income today, and even with Microsoft's faster growth, J&J is still ahead in year 10: $343 vs. $195 on that $10,000. Over the full decade, that's about $2,709 in dividends vs. $1,328.
For Microsoft to match J&J's year-10 income, its dividend would need to grow about 16% a year. At today's rates, it doesn't catch up for about 25 years.
That's a long time to wait.
Coverage doesn't change the answer. On trailing numbers, Microsoft's dividend has more room (a 39.5% cash dividend payout ratio vs. 56.7%). On forward estimates, J&J's does (53.0% vs. 89.2%). Either way, J&J sends the bigger check every year for the next decade.
This isn't to say Microsoft is the worse stock. It may well be the better total-return pick. Consensus has revenue growing 17.8% and 19.5% over the next two fiscal years, it spent $22.27 billion on buybacks over the last twelve months, and it has raised its dividend 17 years in a row.
Microsoft (MSFT): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2024–2029 (TIKR)
If analysts are right, Microsoft adds about $235 billion of yearly revenue by fiscal 2029, nearly twice what J&J is expected to bring in for all of 2029. That's a whole lot of growth.
It's just that the question here is dividend income, and on that one, J&J's head start is too big to overcome.

Microsoft stock best quarter since 1998: Q3 2026 gains 37.5%
Thu, October 1, 2026 at 4:43 AM PDT 2 min read
Microsoft stock surged 37.5% across the third quarter, a performance unmatched since 1998 that lifted the company's market capitalization by $1 trillion, according to Bloomberg. The stock was the fifth-best performer in the Nasdaq 100 Index over that period; the index itself gained just 0.4% over the same three months.
Much of the gain followed Microsoft's earnings report in late July, which showed cloud growth at its fastest pace in four years, driven by demand for AI products. That single-day move of 16% was the stock's strongest showing in nearly two decades, dating back to October 2008, and brought $450 billion in new market value.
The quarterly rally marked a sharp reversal from June, when the stock logged its weakest monthly showing in roughly 25 years amid widespread skepticism about the company's AI outlays and what a world dominated by AI might mean for software vendors.
"After a period where it struggled with the message, Microsoft has been crisper and cleaner on how it will monetize its capital outlay and benefit its customers," said Chad Morganlander, senior portfolio manager at Washington Crossing Advisors, according to Bloomberg. "It is showing a clear path to profitability with AI. As a company that is spending but not going into the red on account, it looks like the adult in the room."
Among the other large AI spenders — Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta — Microsoft is the only one that has not seen free cash flow turn negative on an annual basis, according to Bloomberg.
Wall Street sentiment has shifted. Among the 72 Bloomberg-tracked analysts covering Microsoft, buy ratings account for all but three, and not a single analyst recommends selling the stock. Last week, Stifel analyst Brad Reback upgraded the stock to buy, writing that the company had "clearly turned the corner," according to the outlet.
"Investors realized they misunderstood the company's potential, so a lot of the rally is just the reversal of that mistake," said JoAnne Feeney, portfolio manager at Advisors Capital Management, according to the outlet.
Even after the quarter's outsized move, Microsoft has returned only 6.1% on a year-to-date basis, a figure that falls well short of the Nasdaq 100's 20% advance.

When investors discuss the major artificial intelligence (AI) hyperscalers, Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) sometimes falls to the wayside. However, its Copilot AI platform is rapidly growing and might be its secret weapon in the AI arms race. Copilot is becoming a widely used AI application in the business world, mainly due to its ability to keep companies' internal, proprietary data private. This is becoming an issue for some places, and with Copilot maintaining data security, it's an easy one for IT departments to recommend.
But is it enough to make Microsoft a buy? Let's take a look.
Image source: Getty Images.
Microsoft is benefiting from the AI arms race in three ways
Microsoft has three different ways it can benefit from the AI arms race.
The first, as discussed above, is its Copilot platform. A free version of Copilot is available with all plans, but integrations with some of Microsoft's other apps are a paid add-on. During Microsoft's latest quarter, Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats. That's not an insignificant revenue contributor, and it shows that it's growing in popularity.

Another way Microsoft is benefiting is from its cloud computing service, Azure. Microsoft is spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data center capital expenditures to increase its cloud computing capacity. That's the right move, because there is a monstrous demand backlog. Microsoft's remaining performance obligations rose to $678 billion in the quarter, and it is a reflection of how much computing capacity backlog there is.
A large amount of that is attributed to Microsoft's largest computing client: OpenAI. This is Microsoft's third way to benefit, as it's a major investor in OpenAI. Microsoft is estimated to own about a quarter of OpenAI, which could result in a huge payout if OpenAI goes public later this year.
Those are the three ways Microsoft can benefit from AI, although Copilot may be its most obvious one (and maybe not so secret a weapon). However, I think all three of these avenues combined are an excellent way to approach the AI build-out, and Microsoft is a viable AI investment. However, don't expect it to produce incredible returns, as it's not growing fast enough to mimic some of the faster-growing AI computing companies.

How Much Revenue Visibility Does Microsoft’s Backlog Really Provide?
Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) ended fiscal 2026 with $678 billion of commercial remaining performance obligations. That total offers substantial visibility, but its investment value depends on when revenue arrives, which customers account for it and what Microsoft must spend to serve them. Treating the whole amount as near-term sales would overstate the protection it provides.
At the September 30 market-data snapshot, Microsoft's market capitalization was about $3.86 trillion, around 29 times trailing earnings on an equity basis and roughly 57 times trailing free cash flow. Such a valuation makes the quality and timing of future contracted business more relevant than the size of the headline alone.
How much cash does contracted growth leave after the infrastructure bill? Our Microsoft-versus-Amazon analysis compares the conversion of cloud investment into profit. OpenAI's role adds another question: our examination of the missing profit figure behind Microsoft's large OpenAI revenue stream shows why revenue visibility and shareholder returns need separate tests.
How Much Revenue Visibility Does Microsoft's Backlog Really Provide?
On the July 29 earnings call, management said the weighted average duration of remaining obligations was 2.3 years, with approximately 30% expected to be recognized in the following 12 months. Thirty percent of $678 billion is about $203.4 billion. That is expected recognition from the existing backlog, not an extra $203.4 billion layered on top of the company's normal revenue forecast.
The distinction matters because future revenue also comes from renewals, new contracts and usage that is not captured in the same snapshot. Microsoft's fiscal 2026 revenue was $331.8 billion, spanning businesses beyond this commercial measure. Dividing scheduled backlog recognition by consolidated revenue can give scale, but cannot produce a precise coverage ratio for all future sales.
The backlog grew 84%, while growth excluding OpenAI was 25%. That contrast identifies a source of concentration rather than disproving demand elsewhere. Management said sequential backlog growth came entirely from customers outside frontier labs and that nearly 90% of full-year fiscal 2026 Microsoft Cloud revenue was outside that group. Existing revenue breadth and future contractual concentration can therefore tell different stories.
Contracted revenue still needs profitable capacity
September 15 short interest was 67,346,414 shares, about 0.91% of float, with 3.7 days to cover. The small float percentage makes it weak evidence for a crowded directional trade.
Insider Monkey's hedge fund database recorded 273 Microsoft holders in Q2 2026, down from 282 in Q1. Arrowstreet increased its common-share position 14% to 27,659,541 shares. The divergence between broader participation and one manager's position is historical; it cannot be read as a response to the July 29 backlog disclosure.
Microsoft generated $182.94 billion of operating cash flow in fiscal 2026 and paid $115.95 billion for property and equipment. Simple free cash flow was about $66.99 billion. The approximately $3.81 trillion equity valuation equaled about 57 times that amount, a cash yield near 1.8%.
Backlog can help justify building capacity because it reduces uncertainty about customer demand. It does not remove the equipment cost, energy expense, depreciation or customer-credit exposure. A long contract is more valuable when the associated assets earn good returns throughout its term.
As an illustrative sensitivity, $100 billion of sustainable annual free cash flow would put the current equity value at about 38 times cash flow. At $125 billion, the multiple would be roughly 30.5. Reaching either level requires operating cash growth to exceed the ongoing cash needed for infrastructure, or investment intensity to decline as capacity fills. Neither follows automatically from an 84% increase in obligations.
The strongest bullish case is that Microsoft's broad customer base, contracted demand and expanding cloud platform create both growth and high utilization of new infrastructure. The bearish case is that a larger share of backlog involves expensive, concentrated workloads whose cash returns arrive slowly. If those customers change their deployment plans, long duration may become a risk exposure as well as a source of visibility.
Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) has considerable contracted demand, with recognition timing and customer breadth shaping its value. The backlog becomes more persuasive when deployed capacity converts it into growing cash after investment. Contract growth that consistently outruns cash returns would leave the price dependent on a longer and less certain payoff.

Yes, you can now make New Outlook look like the classic one, although it’s still a web app.
There’s a new optional setting in New Outlook for Windows 11 and Windows 10 that allows you to use this classic design as a “theme.” Microsoft began rolling it out in August 2026, and it finally showed up on my PC.
I went to New Outlook’s Settings > General > Appearance and turned on “Enable classic Outlook style.” Once enabled, New Outlook looked a lot closer to Outlook Classic.
As soon as you tick the box, New Outlook tells you that “some settings aren’t available in classic Outlook style,” and the entire Themes section, including Copilot themes, image backgrounds, and accent colors, gets greyed out. So you can either have the classic look or your custom theme, not both.
That doesn’t change the fact that New Outlook is still a web app running in an Edge-powered container, but it’s also why these themes are so well cooked.
Microsoft can easily customize how New Outlook looks because it’s a website at the end of the day, so a bit of CSS and JavaScript can take you from the new design to the one you loved all these years.

For example, I noticed that the title bar, icons, folder list, and ribbon all changed to look more like the classic version. Even the blue patterned title bar, which is one of the flagship design aspects of New Outlook, is gone. In light mode, it’s replaced with a plain background, again matching the classic version.
Microsoft has also added two small buttons to the top-left corner of the title bar, Send/Receive (sync) and Undo, which mimic Outlook Classic’s Quick Access Toolbar. Even the Outlook logo switches to the older multicolor icon.

Right now, New Outlook has colorful icons, so by just changing the icons and making the background darker, Outlook Classic is being recreated.

“When enabled, the setting applies coordinated changes across the Outlook experience, including visual styling, layout, typography, icons, and selected interactions,” Microsoft explained. “This update is designed to help users who are transitioning from classic Outlook by providing a more familiar experience while maintaining the capabilities of the new Outlook.”

For example, if you’re in the mail view, you can see Send / Receive and Folder tabs alongside File, Home, View, and Help. The blue “New mail” button also becomes a neutral “New Email” button with a separate “New Items” dropdown, and copies Outlook Classic’s iconography.

Microsoft stock climbed on Friday, rising as much as 4% to reach $516.39 in afternoon trading. The move came after Oppenheimer raised its price target on the tech giant and Microsoft rolled out a major overhaul of its Copilot app.
Oppenheimer analyst Brian Schwartz lifted his price target on Microsoft to $570 from $515. He kept his Outperform rating in place. Schwartz pointed to customers increasingly standardizing on Microsoft as their main enterprise AI platform.
Stifel analyst Brad Reback also raised his outlook. He upgraded Microsoft from hold to buy and pushed his price target up to $575 from $530. That target points to roughly 11% upside from Friday’s closing price.

Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna explained the thinking at a preview event. He said the company isn’t trying to build a personal companion app, and instead wants to help people get work done.
The redesigned app centers on three tools. A home hub combines chat with task delegation, letting users edit Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files directly inside the app.
A second tool, built on GitHub Copilot technology, lets non-technical staff build apps and workflows using plain language. It runs inside a sandbox that a company’s IT team controls.
The third tool, called Autopilot, acts as a persistent agent living inside a company’s own cloud setup. It can handle multi-step background tasks without constant human input.

Usage-based billing ties part of that revenue to how often customers actually run the agent tools. That’s a different setup than counting fixed seats each month.

Schwartz flagged some risks alongside his price target increase. He pointed to AI disruption and the possibility that companies pull forward their enterprise tech spending, both of which could weigh on Microsoft’s growth path.
Microsoft’s stock carries a Buy consensus among 55 analysts covering the company, with 14 rating it Strong Buy and 38 rating it Buy. Three analysts rate it Hold.

Microsoft Cloud and AI Strength Fuels Fourth Quarter Results
REDMOND, Wash. — July 29, 2026 — Microsoft Corp. today announced the following results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, as compared to the corresponding period of last fiscal year:
Revenue was $90.0 billion and increased 18% (up 17% in constant currency)
Operating income was $40.6 billion and increased 18%
Net income was $35.8 billion and increased 31% on a GAAP basis, and was $35.3 billion and increased 22% on a non-GAAP basis
Diluted earnings per share was $4.81 and increased 32% on a GAAP basis, and was $4.74 and increased 23% on a non-GAAP basis
Non-GAAP results exclude the impact from investments in OpenAI, explained in the Non-GAAP Definition section below
Several discrete items impacted our financial results in the quarter when compared to our forward-looking guidance provided on April 29, 2026, resulting in a benefit of $0.27 on diluted earnings per share. These include a $3.2 billion gain from our investment in Anthropic and lower-than-expected expenses related to the Voluntary Retirement Program which were partially offset by severance expense and impairment charges in XBOX. When adjusting for these items, we exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income, and diluted earnings per share.
“We are advancing the frontier on the cost-to-outcome curve, ensuring every customer can turn tokens into business results,” said Satya Nadella, chairman and chief executive officer of Microsoft. “This year, Azure revenue surpassed $100 billion for the first time, and Microsoft 365 Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats, reflecting the confidence customers are placing in us to power their AI transformation.”
“We delivered a strong quarter to close out the fiscal year, highlighted by Microsoft Cloud revenue of $59.3 billion, up 27% year-over-year,” said Amy Hood, executive vice president and chief financial officer of Microsoft.

Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenue increased 16% when adjusted for the prior year comparable that benefited from 2 points of in-period revenue recognition. On a reported basis, Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenue increased 14%.

Dynamics 365 revenue increased 13% (up 12% in constant currency)

Azure and other cloud services revenue increased 43%

Windows OEM and Devices revenue decreased 7%

Search advertising revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs increased 10% (up 9% in constant currency)
Microsoft returned $10.2 billion to shareholders in the form of dividends and share repurchases in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2026.

Every quarter Microsoft delivers hundreds of products, services, and enhancements. These releases are driven by years of significant research and development investments, to empower customers with greater productivity, security, and differentiated value.
This momentum is reflected in stories that showcase how our technology is shaping industries and driving customer success. We share innovation updates on our product blogs across Azure, Microsoft 365, and more on our Official Microsoft blog.
